title: Orthogonality gives the closest point
learningObjective: Use orthogonal decomposition to justify projection as a closest-point construction.

retrieve.bodyMarkdown: A basis gives coordinates but does not necessarily measure lengths or angles. What extra structure would let it do so?

encounter.bodyMarkdown: To approximate a point by a point on a line, the shortest connecting segment meets the line at a right angle. How can that picture become a proof?

explain.bodyMarkdown: A real inner product is symmetric and bilinear, with $\langle v,v\rangle>0$ for nonzero $v$. It defines $\|v\|^2=\langle v,v\rangle$ and orthogonality by zero inner product. For a nonzero vector $u$, the projection of $v$ onto its line is $p=\frac{\langle v,u\rangle}{\langle u,u\rangle}u$. Then $v-p$ is orthogonal to $u$. More generally, if $p\in W$ and $v-p\perp W$, for every $w\in W$ the Pythagorean identity gives $\|v-w\|^2=\|v-p\|^2+\|p-w\|^2$. Thus $p$ is the unique closest point in $W$.

reflect.bodyMarkdown: The denominator matters unless the direction vector is unit length. Orthogonality turns an approximation claim into an exact minimization proof.

problems.promptMarkdown: Using the standard dot product, compute $\langle(1,2),(2,-1)\rangle$.

hints.bodyMarkdown: Multiply matching coordinates and add.
Use the standard dot product.
The two products have opposite signs and equal magnitude.
The dot product is $1\cdot2+2(-1)=0$, so the vectors are orthogonal.

problems.solutionMarkdown: The dot product is $1\cdot2+2(-1)=0$, so the vectors are orthogonal.

problems.promptMarkdown: For nonzero $u$, the projection of $v$ onto its span is:

options.label: $\langle v,u\rangle u$ for every $u$.
options.accessibleLabel: langle v,urangle u for every u.

hints.bodyMarkdown: Find a multiple of the direction whose residual is orthogonal.
Set the residual dot product with the direction to zero.
The coefficient must divide by the squared length of the direction.
Write the projection as $cu$ and enforce $(v-cu)\perp u$. Solving gives $c=\langle v,u\rangle/\langle u,u\rangle$.

problems.solutionMarkdown: Write the projection as $cu$ and enforce $(v-cu)\perp u$. Solving gives $c=\langle v,u\rangle/\langle u,u\rangle$.

problems.promptMarkdown: Project $v=(3,1)$ onto the line spanned by $u=(1,1)$. What is the first coordinate of the projection?

hints.bodyMarkdown: Compute the scalar coefficient before reconstructing the vector.
Divide the dot product by the squared length.
The numerator is four and the denominator is two.
The coefficient is $(3+1)/(1+1)=2$. The projection is $(2,2)$, so the first coordinate is two.

problems.solutionMarkdown: The coefficient is $(3+1)/(1+1)=2$. The projection is $(2,2)$, so the first coordinate is two.

problems.promptMarkdown: For the preceding projection $p=(2,2)$ of $v=(3,1)$, enter the two coordinates of the residual $v-p$.

hints.bodyMarkdown: Subtract the projection from the original vector.
Subtraction is coordinatewise.
The first coordinate decreases by two, as does the second.
The residual is $(1,-1)$, and its dot product with $(1,1)$ is zero. This checks the geometric condition.

problems.solutionMarkdown: The residual is $(1,-1)$, and its dot product with $(1,1)$ is zero. This checks the geometric condition.

problems.promptMarkdown: Prove the closest-point property when $p\in W$ and $v-p\perp W$.

steps.textMarkdown: Because $p-w\in W$, the two terms are orthogonal.
The last term is nonnegative and vanishes only for $w=p$, so $p$ is the unique closest point.

hints.bodyMarkdown: Compare the proposed closest point with an arbitrary competitor.
Use the orthogonal decomposition of the error.
The second squared length cannot be negative.
Split the error into orthogonal components. The extra component can only increase the squared distance, strictly unless it is zero.

problems.solutionMarkdown: Split the error into orthogonal components. The extra component can only increase the squared distance, strictly unless it is zero.
